name: Deutsche Bank AG

profile.description: Deutsche Bank is Germany's largest bank, operating Corporate Bank, Investment Bank, Private Bank, and Asset Management (DWS) divisions. Under CEO Christian Sewing, who restructured the bank in 2018–2019 including a retreat from parts of global trading, it has delivered record profits: Q3 2026 profit before tax rose 8% to €2.6B, post-tax profit was ~€1.9B, and nine-month net profit reached an all-time high of €5.9B [1][2][4]. Q3 net revenues rose 4% to ~€8.3B with record Corporate Bank revenues, post-tax RoTE was 10.6%, and the bank targets RoTE above 13% and a cost/income ratio below 60% by 2028 [1]. The dividend has been reinstated and raised each year since 2022 [8].

innovation.label: WEAK
innovation.analysis: Track Record (2/3): Sewing's 2018–2019 restructuring — cutting more than 7,000 jobs and retreating from parts of global trading — transformed a loss-making bank into one reporting a third straight record quarter, with nine-month 2026 net profit at an all-time high of €5.9B [1][4]. AI Deployment (0/2): The research found no specific AI products shipping or quantified AI savings at Deutsche Bank; automation is cited only generally as a reason for back-office cuts [3]. Market Share (1/2): Germany's largest bank, with record Corporate Bank revenues in Q3 2026, but the Investment Bank was broadly flat and no share-gain data was found [1]. Product Pipeline (0/2): No named next-generation products with timelines were found; targets are financial (RoTE >13% by 2028) [1]. R&D Intensity (0/1): No R&D is reported [5].

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (1/4): The search surfaced financial targets (RoTE, cost/income) and cost-cutting, not a distinctive purpose; Deutsche Bank's purpose language is generic for a global bank [1][3]. Community Impact (0/2): No specific community investment programs or dollar amounts were found in this research. Employee Retention (0/2): The bank has run successive rounds of job cuts — more than 7,000 in 2018, a further 2,000 later, and accelerated German branch and back-office cuts in 2025 [3][4]. Insider Buying (0/2): No insider-purchase data was found.

infrastructure.label: STRONG
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored on the Dividend framework (weighted sum 8.559 of 11 = 8/10) [5][6][8]. D/E is excluded as not meaningful for a bank (yfinance returns null). Strengths: forward P/E of 7.3x (1.0), profit margin of 22.7% (1.0), payout ratio of 30% (1.0), and dividend growth since reinstatement (2× weight; 1.0) — the per-ADR dividend rose from $0.21 in 2022 to $1.17 in 2026, a 53% annual rate over four years (5-year CAGR undefined because nothing was paid in 2021, so the 4-year rate is used) [8]. Weaknesses: ROE of 9.0% scores 0.60; Q3 revenue growth of 4% scores 0.80 [1]; the net revenue CAGR of 6.4% (FY2022 €26.7B to FY2025 €32.1B, a 3-year proxy because a 5-year net revenue series was unavailable) scores 0.76 [5]; only 5 consecutive years paid (2× weight; 0.50) and 4 years of growth (0.40) after the 2020–2021 suspension [8]. Liquidity is ample (~$70M daily dollar volume) [6].

ai_resilience.label: MODERATE
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (6/9): Deutsche Bank's core businesses — balance-sheet lending, transaction banking, and capital-markets intermediation — are protected by regulatory licenses, capital requirements, and client relationships that AI cannot replicate [1]. Exposure is real in operations and back-office functions: one research estimate cited in coverage projects banks globally could cut about 200,000 roles over three to five years as AI takes over tasks, and Deutsche has said its cuts would fall mainly on support and back-office staff as it automates [3]. AI is more likely to compress cost/income ratios than to disrupt revenue. AI Opportunity (0/1): No quantified AI revenue was found.

infinite_game.summary: Sinek would credit Christian Sewing's turnaround as an act of leadership — he restructured a failing bank and has delivered three straight record quarters [1][4]. But the bank's story is told in finite terms: RoTE targets, cost/income ratios, and repeated job cuts [1][3]. Its asset manager DWS paid a €25M German greenwashing fine and $25M in SEC penalties after a whistleblower who raised ESG concerns was fired, which Sinek would read as a failure of the Circle of Safety [7]. Deutsche Bank is recovering, but it is optimizing to targets rather than advancing a cause.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (1/3): Public messaging centers on profit, RoTE (>13% by 2028), and cost/income (<60%) targets [1]. No idealistic, service-oriented cause that guides strategy surfaced in the research.

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (0/2): Successive job-cut programs (7,000+ in 2018, 2,000 more later, accelerated branch and back-office cuts in 2025) and the DWS case, where the group sustainability officer who raised concerns was fired before regulators fined DWS, point to a low-trust environment [3][7].

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): No management commentary framing competitors as benchmarks to learn from was found; messaging is about hitting the bank's own targets [1].

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): Deutsche Bank refocused away from global investment banking toward Corporate Bank and Private Bank, and Corporate Bank now posts record revenues [1][4]. The shift was driven by financial necessity and stays within banking.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Sewing's 2018–2019 restructuring took heavy near-term losses and cut over 7,000 jobs to exit unprofitable trading, a costly decision that rebuilt the bank's long-term viability [4]. Since then decisions have been driven by efficiency targets rather than by long-term capability bets.

investment_thesis: Deutsche Bank is a value-priced turnaround that keeps delivering. Q3 2026 profit before tax rose 8% to €2.6B, post-tax profit was ~€1.9B, and nine-month net profit hit an all-time high of €5.9B with a 61.4% cost/income ratio and 11.5% RoTE [1][2]. The shares trade at 7.3x forward earnings and 8.7x trailing [6]. Shareholder returns are growing fast: the per-ADR dividend rose from $0.21 in 2022 to $1.17 in 2026, with a 30% payout ratio and a 3.5% yield [6][8]. Management targets RoTE above 13% and cost/income below 60% by 2028 [1].
thesis_continued: The bear case is mediocre returns and a weak culture record. Q3 RoTE of 10.6% is still below the 2028 target, and ROE is 9.0% [1][6]. Revenue growth is modest (Q3 +4%), and the Investment Bank was broadly flat [1]. The dividend history is short — payments were suspended in 2020–2021 — and DWS paid a €25M greenwashing fine in Germany plus $25M to the SEC ($19M for misleading ESG statements, $6M for AML program failures) [7][8]. Faith alignment is MISALIGNED (Inspire score -67, with Abortion Activism and LGBT Activism as negative attributions and no positives).
key_catalysts: 2028 targets: delivering RoTE above 13% (from 10.6% in Q3 2026) and cost/income below 60% (from 62.4%) would justify a re-rating from 7.3x forward earnings [1][6]
Corporate Bank momentum: record Corporate Bank revenues in Q3 2026 provide stable, fee- and deposit-driven growth less dependent on trading [1]
Rising capital returns: the dividend per ADR rose from $0.77 in 2025 to $1.17 in 2026 with a 30% payout ratio, leaving room for further increases [6][8]
key_risks: Sub-target profitability: Q3 2026 RoTE of 10.6% was slightly below the prior year's 10.7%, and missing the 13% 2028 target would undercut the re-rating thesis [1]
Conduct and regulatory risk: DWS paid a €25M German greenwashing fine and $25M in SEC penalties, including $6M for AML program failures, and further compliance lapses could bring larger penalties [7]
Investment Bank cyclicality: Investment Bank revenues were flat against a record Q3 2025, and a downturn in trading or underwriting would hit group earnings [1]
